sections.title: Recognizing Function Families
sections.learning_target: Students will identify common function families from graphs, equations, tables, and contexts.
i_cans: I can construct evidence for a function family using patterns in graphs, equations, tables, and contexts.
I can apply family features to sort representations into linear, quadratic, exponential, absolute value, and other familiar forms.
I can determine which representation gives the strongest evidence for a function family when features seem similar.

spiral.intro: Identify common function families from graphs, equations, tables, and contexts.
spiral.review: Solve systems graphically and by elimination while interpreting the meaning of different solution types.
spiral.mastery: Analyze and compare linear relationships using multiple representations.

sections.title: Translations
sections.learning_target: Students will graph and write translated functions using key points and key features.
i_cans: I can build translated graphs by moving key points and key features from a parent function.
I can use horizontal and vertical shifts to write equations for translated functions.
I can predict how changing values in an equation moves a graph left, right, up, or down.

spiral.intro: Graph and write translated functions using key points and key features.
spiral.mastery: Graph linear functions and interpret key features.

sections.title: Transformations
sections.learning_target: Students will analyze and graph transformations involving stretches, compressions, and reflections.
i_cans: I can design transformed graphs using stretches, compressions, reflections, and translations of parent functions.
I can apply transformation rules to key points and features across function families.
I can assess whether an equation, graph, or table represents the same transformed function.

spiral.intro: Analyze and graph transformations involving stretches, compressions, and reflections.
spiral.review: Analyze and interpret systems of linear inequalities.
spiral.mastery: Interpret slope as a measure of constant rate of change.

sections.title: Polynomial Operations
sections.learning_target: Students will add, subtract, and multiply polynomial expressions.
i_cans: I can formulate polynomial sums, differences, and products from area, perimeter, and expression contexts.
I can use structure and like terms to add, subtract, and multiply polynomial expressions.
I can extend polynomial operations to equivalent expressions written in different forms.

spiral.intro: Add, subtract, and multiply polynomial expressions.
spiral.review: Solve systems using substitution and choose efficient forms for solving.
spiral.mastery: Write linear equations from graphs, tables, and situations.

sections.title: Polynomial Structure and Quadratic Graphs
sections.learning_target: Students will connect polynomial expressions to quadratic graphs and key features.
i_cans: I can construct connections between polynomial structure, quadratic graphs, and key features.
I can predict graph features from equivalent quadratic expressions.
I can critique whether a polynomial expression supports a claimed vertex, intercept, axis of symmetry, or direction of opening.

spiral.intro: Connect polynomial expressions to quadratic graphs and key features.
spiral.review: Create and solve systems that model real-world situations.
spiral.mastery: Use linear models to represent and interpret real-world data.

4.1.Graph: PLANNED — parent/family graph galleries and graph-based classification appear in WTC, Notes, and every Practice form.
4.1.Equation: PLANNED — recognizable linear, quadratic, exponential, absolute-value, and other familiar equation forms are classified and connected to features.
4.1.Table: PLANNED — constant differences, second differences, ratios, symmetry, and conflicting evidence tables appear in Notes and every Practice form.
4.1.Context: PLANNED — real change patterns are used when family choice affects interpretation.

4.2.Graph: PLANNED — parent/translated overlays and key-point movement appear in WTC, Notes, and every Practice form.
4.2.Equation: PLANNED — transformation form is written and interpreted for horizontal/vertical shifts.
4.2.Table: PLANNED — parent-point to translated-point tables appear in Notes and every Practice form.
4.2.Context: PLANNED — changed baselines/timing benchmarks are used selectively when translation has contextual meaning.

4.3.Graph: PLANNED — parent and stretched/compressed/reflected graphs appear in WTC, Notes, and every Practice form.
4.3.Equation: PLANNED — transformation parameters are connected to vertical scale, reflection, and translation.
4.3.Table: PLANNED — key-point transformation tables appear in Notes and every Practice form.
4.3.Context: PLANNED — scale/reflection changes are interpreted when a genuine model meaning exists.

4.4.Graph: N/A — coordinate graphs are not the natural representation for the polynomial-operation targets.
4.4.Equation: PLANNED — polynomial sums, differences, monomial products, and binomial products are central.
4.4.Table: PLANNED — term-alignment/value tables verify equivalent expressions in every Practice form.
4.4.Context: PLANNED — area/perimeter contexts and rectangle/algebra-tile models make polynomial products meaningful.

4.5.Graph: PLANNED — parabolas with vertices/intercepts/axes appear in WTC, Notes, and every Practice form.
4.5.Equation: PLANNED — standard, factored, and vertex-like forms are connected to visible features.
4.5.Table: PLANNED — quadratic-pattern tables and feature checks appear in Notes and every Practice form.
4.5.Context: PLANNED — simple quadratic models are used when feature meaning matters.
